To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
women had a 3.6-point higher VACS Index score at 1 year than men after adjusting for adherence.
women had worse overall burden of disease scores than men after one year of antiretrovial therapy in VA.
women experienced less improvement than men in overall burden of the disease after 1 year of HIV treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the Veterans Health Administration’s (VHA) HIV/AIDS program on HIV/AIDS-related mortality and morbidity.
understanding sex differences in health and health care among people with HIV infection.
the impact of HIV on the health and functioning of older adults and how this may be modified by other chronic diseases, such as diabetes and heart disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
women experienced a greater burden of disease after one year of ART than men.
there is a significant disparity in the burden of disease in women compared to men after one year of treatment.
women with HIV in VA experience less improvement in their overall burden of disease compared with men with HIV in VA after 1 year on ART.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women experience worse outcomes than men after 12 months of treatment, even after controlling for adherence.
sex disparities exist in burden of disease after ART among HIV-infected patients in VA, but these differences were not due to differences in adherence to ART.
there are sex differences in overall burden of illness among HIV-infected patients in VA after 1 year of HIV treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women with HIV have worse outcomes than men with HIV and that this disparity exists even when women and men are matched on HIV biomarkers.
women have worse outcomes on ART than men.
sex differences in burden of disease are present in the VA, and these differences persist even after adjusting for adherence to HIV treatment.
